# Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions {#sec-loss-functions}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Compute a residual, a sum of squared residuals, a mean squared error and a
  mean absolute error from a set of predictions, in both languages, without
  looking up a formula.
- Say what squaring does to a large error that taking the absolute value does
  not, and show it with a number.
- Evaluate a loss at parameter values of your own choosing, and find the
  parameters that minimise it by searching a grid.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-supervised-learning fitted a line and called it the best fit, without ever
saying best at what. This exercise supplies the missing definition. A loss
function scores a candidate line against the data; the fitting procedure returns
the line with the lowest score. Change the score and you change the line — and
then @sec-gradient-descent asks how the lowest score is found at all.

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

### The same 80 rows

Each chapter is a fresh session, so load the data again.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

diab <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu  <- diab |> filter(glucose > 0) |> slice(1:80) |> select(age, glucose)
```

### One point, one residual

A residual is what the model got wrong for one patient:

$$r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$

Take a line nobody fitted — $\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 120 + 0.5 \times
\text{age}$, invented by hand — and find the patient it serves worst.

```{r}
glu <- glu |> mutate(pred_guess = 120 + 0.5 * age,
                     resid_guess = glucose - pred_guess)

worst <- glu |> slice_max(abs(resid_guess), n = 1)
worst
```

That patient is 58, their measured glucose is 72, the hand-drawn line predicts
149, and the residual is −77 mg/dL — an error larger than the measurement
itself.

```{r}
ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 120, slope = 0.5, colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = age, yend = pred_guess), colour = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)")
```

The red segments are the residuals. A loss function is a rule for turning all
80 of them into one number.

### Four ways to add up 80 mistakes

Residuals are positive and negative, so adding them cancels most of the error
away. Two repairs are in common use, and they are not equivalent.

$$\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \left| r_i \right|$$

Squaring is the L2 loss; taking the absolute value is the L1 loss. The mean
squared error is the sum of squared residuals divided by the number of rows, so
it does not grow simply because the dataset is larger. The root of the MSE —
RMSE — is back in the outcome's units and is easier to quote.

```{r}
loss_table <- function(residuals) {
  m <- length(residuals)              # the number of residuals passed in,
  ssr <- sum(residuals^2)             # not the size of some data frame
  c(SSR = ssr, MSE = ssr / m, RMSE = sqrt(ssr / m),
    MAE = mean(abs(residuals)))
}

round(loss_table(glu$resid_guess), 3)
```

The hand-drawn line scores SSR 90868, MSE 1135.9, RMSE 33.7 and MAE 28.7.
RMSE and MAE are both in mg/dL and the RMSE is the larger of the two, which is
not an accident: squaring weights the worst patients more heavily, so any
summary built from squares sits above the plain average error whenever the
residuals are unequal.

### Task 1 — Score the fitted line against the hand-drawn one

Fit the least-squares line, compute its residuals, and put them through
`loss_table()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
fit_ols   <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)
resid_ols <- ______                     # the residuals of the fitted line
losses    <- loss_table(resid_ols)
round(losses, 3)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`lm()` keeps the residuals for you; `resid()` is the accessor. Subtracting the
predictions from the outcome by hand gives the same vector, and it is worth
doing once to satisfy yourself of that.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
fit_ols   <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)
resid_ols <- resid(fit_ols)
losses    <- loss_table(resid_ols)
round(losses, 3)
```
:::
:::

The fitted line scores MSE 847.5 against the hand-drawn line's 1135.9, and MAE
22.3 against 28.7. It wins on both. That is reassuring but not guaranteed: the
fitted line is the best line *for squared error*, and nothing in the procedure
promises it also has the lowest absolute error. Hold that thought.

### Task 2 — Contaminate three readings

Three glucose values are recorded three times too large — a plausible unit or
transcription error. Multiply rows 1, 3 and 5 by three, refit, and compare.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu_bad <- glu
glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] <- glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] * ______

fit_bad <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = ______)
rbind(clean = coef(fit_ols), contaminated = coef(fit_bad))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
glu_bad <- glu
glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] <- glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] * 3

fit_bad <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu_bad)
rbind(clean = coef(fit_ols), contaminated = coef(fit_bad))
```
:::
:::

Three rows out of eighty — under four per cent of the data — moved the
intercept from 110.3 to 135.3 and turned the slope from +0.289 to −0.136. The
fitted line now says glucose *falls* with age. Nothing warned you; the fit
succeeded, as it always does.

### The result that should bother you

The obvious reading is that outliers break regression. They do not. They break
*this* loss.

Fit the same straight line by minimising mean absolute error instead of mean
squared error. There is no closed form, so hand the loss to a general-purpose
optimiser.

```{r}
fit_lad <- function(data) {
  loss <- function(p) mean(abs(data$glucose - (p[1] + p[2] * data$age)))
  optim(c(mean(data$glucose), 0), loss, method = "Nelder-Mead",
        control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-12))$par
}

glu_bad <- glu
glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] <- glu_bad$glucose[c(1, 3, 5)] * 3

rbind(clean = fit_lad(glu), contaminated = fit_lad(glu_bad))
```

Three steps of reasoning.

1. The least-absolute-error line is intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the clean
   data — and intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the contaminated data. To four
   decimal places, the contamination did not move it at all. Both languages
   agree, having started from the same guess and minimised the same function.
2. Squaring is the mechanism. Tripling a glucose of 194 to 582 multiplies its
   contribution to the MSE by roughly the square of how far out it now is, so
   the line is dragged towards it; under absolute error that patient contributes
   its distance and no more, and three votes out of eighty do not carry.
3. So "the best fit line" is not a property of the data. It is a property of the
   data *and the loss you chose*, and the choice was made for you by whoever
   wrote `lm()`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why squared error anyway
If absolute error is this much more robust, why is every default squared? Two
reasons, and only one of them is about statistics. The squared loss is
differentiable everywhere, which is what lets @sec-gradient-descent follow a
gradient and @sec-ols solve for the answer in closed form; absolute error has a
kink at zero and needs a different class of algorithm. And the mean is the
minimiser of squared error while the median minimises absolute error, so the two
losses are answering different questions about the outcome, not the same
question with different robustness. Convenience, then interpretation — in that
order, historically.
:::

### How the loss changes as the line moves

So far a loss has scored a line someone else supplied. Now treat it as a
function of the parameters, which is what fitting actually optimises:

$$\text{MSE}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}
\left( y_i - \left( \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i \right) \right)^2$$

Start by hand with the first three patients, aged 28, 44 and 26, with glucose
194, 129 and 132. For $\hat\beta_0 = 3$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 5$ the predictions
are 143, 223 and 133, so

$$\frac{(194-143)^2 + (129-223)^2 + (132-133)^2}{3}
 = \frac{2601 + 8836 + 1}{3} = 3812.67$$

### Task 3 — The loss as a function of the parameters

Write that formula as a function and check it against the arithmetic above,
then evaluate it on all 80 rows at two sets of parameters.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
mse_of <- function(beta0, beta1, x, y) {
  mean((y - (______))^2)
}

first3 <- glu |> slice(1:3)
mse_of(3, 5, first3$age, first3$glucose)   # the arithmetic above gave 3812.67

c(at_3_5 = mse_of(3, 5, glu$age, glu$glucose),
  at_4_7 = mse_of(4, 7, glu$age, glu$glucose))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The predicted value for one patient is the intercept plus the slope times that
patient's age. Everything else — the subtraction, the square, the mean — is
already written.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
mse_of <- function(beta0, beta1, x, y) {
  mean((y - (beta0 + beta1 * x))^2)
}

first3 <- glu |> slice(1:3)
mse_of(3, 5, first3$age, first3$glucose)   # the arithmetic above gave 3812.67

c(at_3_5 = mse_of(3, 5, glu$age, glu$glucose),
  at_4_7 = mse_of(4, 7, glu$age, glu$glucose))
```
:::
:::

On all 80 rows those two candidates score 7462 and 22991 against the fitted
line's 847.5. Both are terrible, and the first is better than the second, which
is all a loss is for: ranking candidates.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Which number is the intercept
Writing $\hat\beta_0 = 3$, $\hat\beta_1 = 5$ and then drawing
`geom_abline(slope = 3, intercept = 5)` plots a different line from the one you
scored, and the plot will look convincing. `geom_abline()` takes `slope` and
`intercept` by name for exactly this reason. Name both arguments, every time.
:::

### The whole surface at once

Evaluate the MSE over a grid of candidate parameter values — 101 intercepts
between 60 and 160, 151 slopes between −1 and 2, 15,251 lines in total — and
draw the result. The red point is what `lm()` returned.

```{r}
mse_of  <- function(beta0, beta1, x, y) mean((y - (beta0 + beta1 * x))^2)
fit_ols <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

grid <- expand_grid(b0 = seq(60, 160, by = 1),
                    b1 = seq(-1, 2, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(MSE = map2_dbl(b0, b1, ~ mse_of(.x, .y, glu$age, glu$glucose)))

ggplot(grid, aes(x = b0, y = b1)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = log10(MSE))) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = log10(MSE)), colour = "white", alpha = 0.4, bins = 12) +
  annotate("point", x = coef(fit_ols)[[1]], y = coef(fit_ols)[[2]],
           colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[0]), y = expression(hat(beta)[1]),
       fill = "log10(MSE)")
```

Two features of that picture matter for the next exercise. The surface is a
bowl: it has one lowest point and no others, which is why least squares has a
single answer. And the bowl is a long diagonal trough rather than a round basin,
because the intercept and the slope trade off against each other — raise the
slope and you can compensate by lowering the intercept. @sec-gradient-descent
walks downhill on this exact surface, and the shape of the trough is what makes
that harder than it sounds.

### Task 4 — Find the minimum by brute force

Pull the lowest cell out of the grid you just built and compare it with the
fitted line.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
best <- grid |> slice_min(______, n = 1)
best

coef(fit_ols)   # the fitted line, to compare
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`slice_min()` takes the name of the column to minimise, unquoted.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
best <- grid |> slice_min(MSE, n = 1)
best

coef(fit_ols)   # the fitted line, to compare
```
:::
:::

The grid's best cell is intercept 110, slope 0.30, with an MSE of 847.55 —
against `lm()`'s 110.298, 0.2887 and 847.52. The difference is the spacing of
the grid and nothing else.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not just use the grid
Fifteen thousand evaluations to recover two numbers already feels wasteful, and
it is: the grid also has to be centred near the answer to find it, which
requires knowing the answer. With ten parameters rather than two, a grid of this
resolution would need more evaluations than there are atoms in the room. Grid
search is a teaching device here, not a method.
:::

## Python

### The same 80 rows

Each chapter is a fresh session, so load the data again.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80)
           .reset_index(drop=True))
```

### One point, one residual

A residual is what the model got wrong for one patient:

$$r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$

Take a line nobody fitted — $\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 120 + 0.5 \times
\text{age}$, invented by hand — and find the patient it serves worst.

```{python}
glu["pred_guess"] = 120 + 0.5 * glu["age"]
glu["resid_guess"] = glu["glucose"] - glu["pred_guess"]

worst = glu.loc[[glu["resid_guess"].abs().idxmax()]]
worst
```

That patient is 58, their measured glucose is 72, the hand-drawn line predicts
149, and the residual is −77 mg/dL — an error larger than the measurement
itself.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.6)
ax.vlines(glu["age"], glu["pred_guess"], glu["glucose"], color="red", alpha=0.3)
ax.plot(glu["age"], glu["pred_guess"], color="darkorange")
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)"); ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
plt.show()
```

The red segments are the residuals. A loss function is a rule for turning all
80 of them into one number.

### Four ways to add up 80 mistakes

Residuals are positive and negative, so adding them cancels most of the error
away. Two repairs are in common use, and they are not equivalent.

$$\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \left| r_i \right|$$

Squaring is the L2 loss; taking the absolute value is the L1 loss. The mean
squared error is the sum of squared residuals divided by the number of rows, so
it does not grow simply because the dataset is larger. The root of the MSE —
RMSE — is back in the outcome's units and is easier to quote.

```{python}
def loss_table(residuals):
    residuals = np.asarray(residuals)
    m = len(residuals)
    ssr = np.sum(residuals**2)
    return {"SSR": ssr, "MSE": ssr / m, "RMSE": np.sqrt(ssr / m),
            "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(residuals))}

{k: round(v, 3) for k, v in loss_table(glu["resid_guess"]).items()}
```

The hand-drawn line scores SSR 90868, MSE 1135.9, RMSE 33.7 and MAE 28.7.
RMSE and MAE are both in mg/dL and the RMSE is the larger of the two, which is
not an accident: squaring weights the worst patients more heavily, so any
summary built from squares sits above the plain average error whenever the
residuals are unequal.

### Task 1 — Score the fitted line against the hand-drawn one

Fit the least-squares line, compute its residuals, and put them through
`loss_table()`.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"]
fit_ols   = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
resid_ols = ______                      # the residuals of the fitted line
losses    = loss_table(resid_ols)
print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in losses.items()})
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"]
fit_ols   = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
resid_ols = y - fit_ols.predict(X)
losses    = loss_table(resid_ols)
print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in losses.items()})
```
:::
:::

The fitted line scores MSE 847.5 against the hand-drawn line's 1135.9, and MAE
22.3 against 28.7. It wins on both. That is reassuring but not guaranteed: the
fitted line is the best line *for squared error*, and nothing in the procedure
promises it also has the lowest absolute error. Hold that thought.

### Task 2 — Contaminate three readings

Three glucose values are recorded three times too large — a plausible unit or
transcription error. Multiply rows 1, 3 and 5 by three, refit, and compare.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] = glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] * ______

fit_bad = LinearRegression().fit(glu_bad[["age"]], ______)
{"clean": (fit_ols.intercept_, fit_ols.coef_[0]),
 "contaminated": (fit_bad.intercept_, fit_bad.coef_[0])}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
R counts rows from 1 and pandas from 0, so rows 1, 3 and 5 are `[0, 2, 4]` in
Python. This is the one indexing difference that silently changes a result
rather than raising an error.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] = glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] * 3

fit_bad = LinearRegression().fit(glu_bad[["age"]], glu_bad["glucose"])
{"clean": (fit_ols.intercept_, fit_ols.coef_[0]),
 "contaminated": (fit_bad.intercept_, fit_bad.coef_[0])}
```
:::
:::

Three rows out of eighty — under four per cent of the data — moved the
intercept from 110.3 to 135.3 and turned the slope from +0.289 to −0.136. The
fitted line now says glucose *falls* with age. Nothing warned you; the fit
succeeded, as it always does.

### The result that should bother you

The obvious reading is that outliers break regression. They do not. They break
*this* loss.

Fit the same straight line by minimising mean absolute error instead of mean
squared error. There is no closed form, so hand the loss to a general-purpose
optimiser.

```{python}
from scipy.optimize import minimize

def fit_lad(data):
    loss = lambda p: np.mean(np.abs(data["glucose"] - (p[0] + p[1] * data["age"])))
    return minimize(loss, [data["glucose"].mean(), 0.0], method="Nelder-Mead",
                    options={"maxiter": 5000, "fatol": 1e-12, "xatol": 1e-10}).x

glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] = glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] * 3

{"clean": fit_lad(glu), "contaminated": fit_lad(glu_bad)}
```

Three steps of reasoning.

1. The least-absolute-error line is intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the clean
   data — and intercept 101.9, slope 0.4375 on the contaminated data. To four
   decimal places, the contamination did not move it at all. Both languages
   agree, having started from the same guess and minimised the same function.
2. Squaring is the mechanism. Tripling a glucose of 194 to 582 multiplies its
   contribution to the MSE by roughly the square of how far out it now is, so
   the line is dragged towards it; under absolute error that patient contributes
   its distance and no more, and three votes out of eighty do not carry.
3. So "the best fit line" is not a property of the data. It is a property of the
   data *and the loss you chose*, and the choice was made for you by whoever
   wrote `LinearRegression`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why squared error anyway
If absolute error is this much more robust, why is every default squared? Two
reasons, and only one of them is about statistics. The squared loss is
differentiable everywhere, which is what lets @sec-gradient-descent follow a
gradient and @sec-ols solve for the answer in closed form; absolute error has a
kink at zero and needs a different class of algorithm. And the mean is the
minimiser of squared error while the median minimises absolute error, so the two
losses are answering different questions about the outcome, not the same
question with different robustness. Convenience, then interpretation — in that

:::

$$\text{MSE}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}

Start by hand with the first three patients, aged 28, 44 and 26, with glucose

are 143, 223 and 133, so

$$\frac{(194-143)^2 + (129-223)^2 + (132-133)^2}{3}

### The whole surface at once

Evaluate the MSE over a grid of candidate parameter values — 101 intercepts
between 60 and 160, 151 slopes between −1 and 2, 15,251 lines in total — and
draw the result. The red point is what `LinearRegression` returned.

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
fit_ols = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"])

def mse_of(beta0, beta1, x, y):
    return np.mean((y - (beta0 + beta1 * x))**2)

b0_vals = np.arange(60, 160.001, 1.0)
b1_vals = np.arange(-1, 2.0001, 0.02)
B0, B1 = np.meshgrid(b0_vals, b1_vals, indexing="ij")
resid_grid = glu["glucose"].values - (B0[..., None] + B1[..., None] * glu["age"].values)
MSE = (resid_grid**2).mean(axis=-1)       # average over patients, not parameters

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cs = ax.contourf(B0, B1, np.log10(MSE), levels=20, cmap="magma")
ax.scatter([fit_ols.intercept_], [fit_ols.coef_[0]], color="red", zorder=3)
cbar = fig.colorbar(cs, ax=ax, label="log10(MSE)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\hat\beta_0$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\hat\beta_1$")
plt.show()
```

Two features of that picture matter for the next exercise. The surface is a
bowl: it has one lowest point and no others, which is why least squares has a
single answer. And the bowl is a long diagonal trough rather than a round basin,
because the intercept and the slope trade off against each other — raise the
slope and you can compensate by lowering the intercept. @sec-gradient-descent
walks downhill on this exact surface, and the shape of the trough is what makes
that harder than it sounds.

### Task 4 — Find the minimum by brute force

Pull the lowest cell out of the grid you just built and compare it with the
fitted line.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
i, j = np.unravel_index(MSE.______(), MSE.shape)
print(b0_vals[i], b1_vals[j], MSE[i, j])

print(round(fit_ols.intercept_, 3), round(fit_ols.coef_[0], 4))   # the fitted line, to compare
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
You want the position of the smallest value in a 2-D array, which numpy gives
you as a flat index; `unravel_index` is already there to turn it back into a
row and a column.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
i, j = np.unravel_index(MSE.argmin(), MSE.shape)
print(b0_vals[i], b1_vals[j], MSE[i, j])

print(round(fit_ols.intercept_, 3), round(fit_ols.coef_[0], 4))   # the fitted line, to compare
```
:::
:::

The grid's best cell is intercept 110, slope 0.30, with an MSE of 847.55 —
against `LinearRegression`'s 110.298, 0.2887 and 847.52. The difference is the spacing of
the grid and nothing else.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not just use the grid
Fifteen thousand evaluations to recover two numbers already feels wasteful, and
it is: the grid also has to be centred near the answer to find it, which
requires knowing the answer. With ten parameters rather than two, a grid of this
resolution would need more evaluations than there are atoms in the room. Grid
search is a teaching device here, not a method.
:::

::::::

## Reflection

1. A colleague reports an RMSE of 29.1 mg/dL and a MAE of 22.3 mg/dL for the
   same model and asks which is the real error. What do you say?
2. You are predicting length of stay so that a bed manager can plan tomorrow's
   discharges. Give one argument for scoring that model with absolute error and
   one for squared error, and say which you would defend to the bed manager.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** Reflection 1: both are real and they measure different things —
RMSE exceeds MAE whenever the residuals are unequal, and the gap between them is
itself a description of the error distribution. Neither is "the" error; the
question to ask back is what decision the number is for. Reflection 2: absolute
error treats a one-day and a ten-day miss proportionally, which matches a
planner counting beds; squared error says a ten-day miss is far worse than ten
one-day misses, which matches a service where a single badly wrong case causes a
cancellation. The defensible answer names the decision, not the formula.

**Expected values** (regenerated data varies in the last digit). Hand-drawn line
$120 + 0.5x$: SSR ≈ 90,000–91,000, MSE ≈ 1130–1140, MAE ≈ 28–29. Fitted line:
MSE ≈ 845–850, MAE ≈ 22–23. Contaminated fit: intercept ≈ 134–136, slope ≈ −0.14
(the sign flip is the point). Least-absolute-error fit: ≈ 101.9 and ≈ 0.44, the
same to four decimals before and after contamination. Grid minimum: intercept
110, slope 0.30, MSE ≈ 847.6.

**Common failures.** (1) Using row indices 1, 3, 5 in pandas, which contaminates
different patients and gives different coefficients — worth letting them hit,
then asking why the two languages disagree. (2) Dividing the SSR by a hard-coded
80 rather than by `length(residuals)`, which is silently wrong the moment the
function is reused; the original version of this material had exactly that bug.
(3) Expecting the optimiser to return the same two decimals every time — it is
Nelder-Mead, and the answer here happens to be stable, but say that it is not
guaranteed.

**Plenary.** Put the clean and contaminated coefficient tables side by side and
ask which line a clinician should be shown. Then reveal the
least-absolute-error numbers. The reaction to the slope not moving at all is the
moment the day's argument lands.

**Timing.** Task 4's grid takes a few seconds to evaluate in R. If you are
short, show the surface plot and discuss it rather than having everyone build
the grid; the plot is the part they remember.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Where does the squared loss put the line
Contaminate a single patient rather than three, and increase the multiplier
from 1 to 10 in steps, refitting each time. Plot the fitted slope against the
multiplier. The relationship is close to linear, and it has no breakpoint: there
is no size of error at which squared loss decides to ignore a point.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — A loss that is neither
Huber loss is squared for small residuals and absolute for large ones. Write it,
minimise it with `optim()` or `minimize()` on the contaminated data, and find
the value of its cut-off at which the fitted slope flips back to positive. That
number is the amount of contamination you have implicitly assumed.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can compute any of the standard regression losses from
residuals, state what each does with a badly mispredicted patient, and
demonstrate that the best fit line depends on which loss was chosen.

**Cannot:** that you can find the minimum of a loss for any model worth fitting.
A grid of 15,251 candidates found two parameters approximately. @sec-gradient-descent
replaces the grid with a method that uses the slope of the loss itself.
